My research focuses on human-centered artificial intelligence, scientific reasoning, and self-regulated learning. I investigate educational feedback, teachers' technology adoption, and research-informed instructional change. I have coordinated a published four-university experiment and supervise master's and doctoral research.

My work examines direct, reflective, and hybrid generative-AI feedback and the conditions in which technological support improves scientific reasoning rather than merely improving an AI-assisted product. A central concern is whether learners maintain evaluative judgement and argument quality when support is removed.

This strand focuses on evidence-based scientific argumentation, inquiry, feedback uptake, revision processes, and self-regulated learning. Experimental approaches evaluate learning outcomes and transfer across contexts, including delayed assessments.

Research integrates virtual and augmented reality, educational robotics, intelligent tutoring, and gamification. I investigate both instructional effectiveness and educators' technology adoption using theory-driven quantitative models.

A pretest–posttest quasi-experiment with a control group examined middle school science learning.
The combined system showed more favourable learning, motivation, engagement and confidence outcomes in the reported comparison.

Scope note · editorial interpretation. The intervention combines several features; the comparison does not isolate the effect of augmented reality alone. The publisher states that the data are not public and requests are subject to approvals.

Cluster-randomized, longitudinal comparison across four universities: 1,176 first-year students in 48 course sections.

Direct AI-supported feedback improved immediate argument gains relative to peer feedback. Reflective and hybrid designs performed better than direct feedback on delayed AI-free transfer. The hybrid condition also showed a clearer conceptual-learning advantage; the reflective-versus-direct conceptual-learning contrast was not significant.

Scope note · editorial interpretation. The comparison concerns particular instructional designs in university science courses. It is not evidence that every reflective prompt, AI system or classroom implementation will reproduce these outcomes.

Four-week quasi-experimental comparison involving 59 eighth-grade students: 29 in self-regulated flipped learning and 30 in conventional flipped learning.
The self-regulated condition performed better on the reported achievement, attitude, self-regulation and motivation measures.
Scope note · editorial interpretation. A small, short-duration quasi-experiment does not establish the same effect across all schools, topics or longer periods.
